Data Analyst | Healthcare Analytics | Business Intelligence | Healthcare RCM Specialist → Data Analyst | Power BI, SQL, Python | Sharing insights on data analysis, Healthcare data & revenue analytics
 
I am a Certified Data Analyst with 6.5+ years of professional experience combining strong domain expertise in US Healthcare Revenue Cycle Management (RCM) with modern data analytics skills.
 
My career began in US Healthcare, where I worked extensively in medical billing, claims management, denial analysis, payment reconciliation, reporting, and operational process improvement. Working with large volumes of business data developed my analytical mindset and sparked my interest in solving problems through data.
 
Since October 2022, I have been focused on transitioning into Data Analytics through structured learning, professional certifications, internship experience, and hands-on portfolio projects. During this period, I built practical expertise in SQL, Power BI (DAX), Python, and Advanced Excel while developing dashboards, performing exploratory data analysis, and transforming raw data into meaningful business insights.
 
I completed a Data Analyst Internship with MeriSKILL, where I worked on data cleaning, visualization, dashboard development, and reporting using real-world datasets.
 
My portfolio includes analytics projects across Healthcare, Sales, E-commerce, Customer Analytics, and Operations, demonstrating the ability to apply analytical thinking across multiple business domains.

My core Skills are:

 • Python

• Dashboard Development

I continuously invest in learning emerging technologies, including AI-powered analytics tools, to stay aligned with evolving business needs.
 
I am looking for opportunities as a Data Analyst, Healthcare Data Analyst, Business Analyst, or BI Analyst to combine business knowledge with data-driven decision-making to create measurable business impact.

🏥 Healthcare Revenue Cycle Analytics | Day 14
Payment Posting & Reconciliation — Did We Receive What We Expected?
The payer processed the claim.
Now the payment has arrived.
But the RCM process is not finished.
The next important question is:
Did the payment we received match what we expected?
Payment posting is the process of recording the payer's payment and related claim-level financial information in the billing system.
Reconciliation goes one step further.
It helps us compare the payment information received with the related billing and expected payment information to identify differences that need investigation.
For example:
Claim submitted: $1,000
Expected payer payment: $800
Actual payer payment: $650
At first, we know there is a $150 difference.
But we should not immediately call that $150 an underpayment.
We need to ask:
🔹 Was there a contractual adjustment?
🔹 Was part of the amount assigned to patient responsibility?
🔹 Was the claim partially paid?
🔹 Was there a denial or adjustment on one line?
🔹 Was the expected amount calculated correctly?
🔹 Does the payer's remittance explain the difference?
This is where an RCM Data Analyst can move from “payment reporting” to “payment investigation.”
For example, we might discover:
Payer A → 98% of expected payment
Payer B → 96%
Payer C → 82% 🚨
Now the question becomes:
Why is Payer C showing a much larger payment variance?
We can investigate by:
📌 Payer
📌 Service
📌 Procedure
📌 Provider
📌 Location
📌 Contract
📌 Adjustment reason
📌 Time period
The goal is not simply to record the money received.
The goal is to understand whether the payment was accurately posted, properly reconciled, and consistent with what should have been received under the applicable rules.
This is where payment data becomes Revenue Intelligence.
In the handwritten notes, I will break down payment posting, reconciliation, remittance information, payment vs adjustment vs patient responsibility, payment variance, RCM Analyst questions, RCM Data Analyst investigation, and KPI/formula logic.

🏥 Healthcare Revenue Cycle Analytics | Day 13
Claim Adjudication — What Happens After the Payer Receives the Claim?
A claim has been created, reviewed, and submitted.
Now it reaches the payer.
But submission does not mean payment is guaranteed.
The payer still needs to process the claim and determine how the service will be handled according to the patient's coverage, the claim information, and the applicable payer rules.
This process is known as claim adjudication.
The payer may determine that the claim should be:
✅ Paid
 🟡 Paid differently than expected
 ❌ Denied
 🔄 Adjusted
 ⏳ Held or require additional information
This is where the RCM Data Analyst needs to look beyond:
“How many claims were paid?”
A better question is:
“Why did the payer make this particular payment or denial decision?”
Consider this example:
A hospital submits 10,000 claims.
8,900 are paid
 700 are denied
 400 require further processing or adjustment
The overall result tells us what happened.
But it does not tell us why.
So we investigate:
🔹 Which payer has the highest denial rate?
🔹 Which services are most frequently denied?
🔹 What are the major denial reasons?
🔹 Are denials related to eligibility, authorization, coding, documentation, or other issues?
🔹 Are payments different from what was expected?
🔹 Are certain denial reasons increasing over time?
🔹 Are the same issues coming back repeatedly?
Now imagine:
Overall Denial Rate = 7%
That number may look manageable.
But after segmentation:
Payer A → 3%
 Payer B → 5%
 Payer C → 14% 🚨
The next question is not:
“Why is our denial rate 7%?”
It becomes:
“What is happening with Payer C that is different from the rest?”
This is where claim adjudication becomes a Revenue Intelligence problem.
The analyst connects:
Claim Submitted → Payer Decision → Payment / Denial → Reason → Root Cause → Action
The objective is not simply to report the payer's decision.
It is to understand what drove that decision and whether the organization can prevent similar outcomes in the future.
In the handwritten notes, I will explain what claim adjudication means, how the payer processes a claim, the major outcomes and terminology, what an RCM Analyst should investigate, what an RCM Data Analyst should analyze, and the KPI and formula logic used to understand payer outcomes.

🏥 Healthcare Revenue Cycle Analytics | Day 12
Claim Scrubbing, Validation & Submission — Is the Claim Really Ready to Go?
A claim has been created.
The patient information is available.
The charges have been captured.
The coding has been completed.
But before the claim is sent to the payer, there is another important question:
Is the claim complete, consistent, and ready for submission?
This is where claim scrubbing and validation become important.
Claim validation is not simply about checking whether a claim exists. It is about identifying information that may be missing, inconsistent, or outside the defined billing requirements before the claim is submitted.
For example, a claim may have been created successfully, but an analyst may still need to investigate:
🔹 Does the patient information match the encounter?
🔹 Does the payer information match the applicable coverage?
🔹 Do the procedure and diagnosis information align with the underlying records?
🔹 Are the required claim details present?
🔹 Are there duplicate or conflicting claim records?
🔹 Are there known billing edits that need to be resolved?
🔹 Are there claims repeatedly returning to the billing team for correction?
Now consider this:
10,000 claims were created.
9,400 passed the defined validation checks.
600 require review.
The important question is not simply:
“Why did 600 claims fail validation?”
We should investigate what type of problem those 600 claims contain and where the pattern is concentrated.
For example:
Payer A → 3% exceptions
 Payer B → 4% exceptions
 Payer C → 12% exceptions 🚨
Now the investigation moves deeper:
Payer C
 ↓
 Specific Service
 ↓
 Specific Exception
 ↓
 Root Cause
This is where an RCM Data Analyst can add value.
Instead of treating every claim exception as an individual problem, the analyst can identify patterns that may point to a process, data, payer, or workflow issue.
The objective is not simply to submit claims quickly.
It is to submit clean and accurate claims that correctly represent the underlying patient encounter.
In the handwritten notes, I will explain what claim scrubbing and validation mean, why they are performed, what happens before and after submission, common claim exceptions, the questions an RCM Analyst should ask, the questions an RCM Data Analyst should investigate, and the KPI and formula logic used to measure the process.

🏥 Healthcare Revenue Cycle Analytics | Day 11
Medical Billing & Claim Creation — When Does an Encounter Become a Claim?
The patient received the service.
The service was documented.
The charge was captured.
The medical coding was completed.
But the revenue cycle still has an important step:
How do we bring all of this information together to create a claim?
Medical billing connects information from different parts of the patient encounter, including patient details, insurance information, provider information, diagnosis and procedure codes, charges, dates of service, and other required claim information.
A claim is not simply a collection of data.
It should accurately represent what happened during the patient encounter and what is being requested from the payer for payment.
Consider this situation:
A procedure was performed and documented.
 The charge was captured.
 The code was assigned.
But when the claim is created, some information does not match the underlying records.
Now the important question is not:
“Was the claim created?”
It is:
“Does the claim accurately represent the encounter?”
An RCM Data Analyst should be able to connect:
Encounter → Documentation → Charge → Coding → Claim
and investigate where information may be missing, inconsistent, or different from the underlying records.
For example, an analyst may ask:
Does the patient information match the encounter?
Does the payer information match the verified coverage?
Do the procedures and diagnoses match the coded record?
Do the claim charges match the captured charges?
Does the provider information match the encounter?
Are required claim elements available?
Are similar inconsistencies occurring repeatedly?
This is where RCM analytics becomes more than reporting.
The objective is not simply to know how many claims were created.
The objective is to understand whether those claims accurately represent the services provided and whether the information is ready for the next stage of the revenue cycle.
In the handwritten notes, I will explain the claim creation process, key terminology, major claim data elements, how information flows from the encounter into the claim, RCM Analyst questions, RCM Data Analyst investigation, and KPI/formula logic.

🏥 Healthcare Revenue Cycle Analytics | Day 10
Clinical Documentation & Medical Coding — Did the Record Support the Claim?
A service may have been performed and the charge may have been captured.
But before that information becomes a claim, another important question needs to be answered:
Does the documentation support what is being billed?
Clinical documentation records the patient's care, services, findings, procedures, and other information needed to support the encounter.
Medical coding then translates the documented clinical information into the appropriate standardized codes according to applicable coding guidelines.
This creates an important connection:
Service Performed
 ↓
 Documentation
 ↓
 Charge Capture
 ↓
 Coding
 ↓
 Claim
Now consider a simple situation.
A procedure was performed and a charge was captured.
But the documentation does not contain enough information to support the coded service.
The problem is no longer simply:
“Was the charge captured?”
The better question becomes:
“Does the documentation support the service and coding represented on the claim?”
An RCM Data Analyst can investigate patterns such as:
• Which services have the highest documentation-related exceptions?
• Are documentation issues concentrated by provider, department, or location?
• How often are charges held because documentation is incomplete?
• Are coding changes occurring frequently after initial review?
• Are certain services producing more coding-related rework?
• Are documentation and coding exceptions increasing over time?
The important analytical connection is:
Service → Documentation → Charge → Code → Claim
If these elements do not align, the downstream claim may require correction, additional review, or other action.
The objective is not simply to measure how many claims were coded.
It is to understand whether the clinical record, captured charge, and coded claim tell a consistent story.
In the handwritten notes, I will explain the basic terminology, documentation-to-coding workflow, key data elements, RCM Analyst questions, RCM Data Analyst investigation points, and KPI/formula logic.
